Walk me through your DevOps or DevSecOps: Structure around the specific overlap between your background and the role's stated requirements - name the shared technologies/practices explicitly (e.g. if the JD emphasizes GKE and security, lead with your GKE and security-relevant work), then close with one concrete project demonstrating that overlap in action, tailoring the emphasis to what this specific role actually needs rather than reciting a generic career summary.
What hands-on experience do you have wit: Answer with actual scope - cluster count/scale, whether you managed cluster lifecycle (upgrades, node pools) or primarily deployed workloads onto existing clusters, and one concrete production issue you've resolved on GKE specifically - calibrated honesty here sets up accurate follow-up depth.
A production pod in GKE is stuck in Cras: `kubectl get pods` to confirm the state and restart count, `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` to see the crashed container's last output before it died, `kubectl describe pod` for the exit code and recent events (OOMKilled = 137, application error, failed dependency). Correlate with what changed in the deployment (new image, new config, new resource limits) since a CrashLoopBackOff immediately following a deploy is almost always caused by that specific change - roll back first to restore service if impact is significant, then debug the new version separately.
How would you design and maintain a high: Use a regional cluster (control plane and nodes spread across zones) for HA, HPA/Cluster Autoscaler for elastic capacity, PodDisruptionBudgets to protect availability during voluntary disruptions (upgrades, scaling), multi-zone node pools with topology spread constraints to avoid single-zone concentration, and a full observability stack (metrics, logs, traces) with SLO-based alerting - resilience comes from designing for failure at every layer (a zone can go down, a node can fail, a Pod can crash) rather than assuming any single layer is infallible.
A RHEL/Linux server has high CPU, low di: Triage by severity/dependency - disk space issues often cascade into service failures (a service can't write logs/data and crashes), so check `df -h`/`du -sh` first and free space if critical (rotate/compress logs, clear temp files) before diagnosing anything else, since a full disk can make every other diagnostic step (writing new logs, restarting services) unreliable. Then check `top`/`ps aux` for the CPU-consuming process and `systemctl status`/`journalctl -u <service>` for why specific services are failing - restore services in dependency order (databases/core services before dependents) once the underlying resource issue is cleared.
You are on-call during a major outage af: Detection: confirm via dashboards/alerts and assess actual customer impact scope. Mitigation: prioritize restoring service (rollback, scale, failover) over full root-causing when customer satisfaction is directly affected. Communication: post regular status updates on a fixed cadence to stakeholders (even 'still investigating' beats silence), and keep customer-facing status appropriately abstracted. Escalation: bring in the right specialists early if the cause isn't quickly apparent, rather than one person struggling alone under time pressure. RCA: once resolved, build a factual timeline, identify the true root cause, and assign concrete owned follow-up actions.
How do you plan and execute production c: Follow a formal change management process - a documented change request with risk assessment, a rollback plan defined before execution (not improvised if something goes wrong), a defined maintenance window if downtime risk exists, required approvals from relevant stakeholders (and security/compliance sign-off where regulation demands it), and post-change validation confirming the system is healthy before closing the change - regulated environments require this audit trail to exist and be followed consistently, not just for critical changes.
Design a CI/CD pipeline using GitHub, JI: A commit linked to a JIRA ticket (enforced via commit message conventions or a Jenkins/JIRA integration) triggers Jenkins via GitHub webhook - build, unit test, and security scan stages run automatically; Ansible handles the configuration/deployment step onto target servers/environments; production deployment requires a manual approval gate in Jenkins tied to the JIRA ticket's approval status; rollback is a re-run of the Ansible playbook targeting the previous known-good artifact version. Auditability comes from the JIRA ticket linking business justification to the specific Jenkins build/deployment record, giving a full traceable chain from requirement to production change.
How have you used Terraform and Ansible: Terraform provisions the infrastructure itself (VMs, networks, load balancers, managed services) - the boundary is that Terraform should own anything represented as a distinct cloud resource. Ansible then handles configuration within that provisioned infrastructure (installing packages, deploying application code, managing config files, orchestrating multi-step processes) - the boundary is anything that happens *inside* an already-provisioned resource rather than creating/destroying the resource itself. Terraform's `local-exec` or a CI step commonly triggers an Ansible run against newly provisioned hosts as the handoff point between the two.
How would you implement secrets manageme: Use the External Secrets Operator (or Vault's own Kubernetes auth integration/sidecar injector) so Kubernetes Secrets are synced from Vault/Secret Manager at runtime rather than being hand-created or committed anywhere - applications authenticate to Vault using their Kubernetes service account identity (Vault's Kubernetes auth method), receiving only the specific secrets their policy grants access to, with automatic rotation propagating to running Pods without a manual redeploy in many configurations.
Compare Deployment, StatefulSet, and Dae: Deployment for stateless, interchangeable workloads (most application services) where any replica can be freely replaced. StatefulSet for workloads needing stable identity and per-replica persistent storage (databases, message queues) where replica ordering and identity matter. DaemonSet for node-level agents that must run on every node (log collectors, monitoring exporters, security/EDR agents) - an enterprise platform typically uses all three simultaneously for their respective workload categories, not one exclusively.
How would you use Splunk, AppDynamics, a: Splunk for centralized log search/analysis and building alerts on log-pattern anomalies, AppDynamics for application performance monitoring (transaction tracing, code-level bottleneck identification), and xMatters for intelligent alert routing/escalation (reducing noise by correlating and de-duplicating alerts, and escalating automatically if the primary on-call doesn't acknowledge in time) - together these cover detection (Splunk/AppDynamics surfacing the problem) and response (xMatters ensuring the right person is notified appropriately rather than everyone getting paged for everything).
What SQL or database troubleshooting exp: For connectivity: confirm network path/firewall rules first, then check the database's own connection limits (`max_connections` exhaustion is a common cause masquerading as a network issue). For slow queries: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (PostgreSQL) or execution plan analysis (MSSQL) to find missing indexes or poor query plans. For locks: query the database's own lock/blocking views (`pg_locks`/`pg_stat_activity` in PostgreSQL, `sys.dm_tran_locks` in MSSQL) to identify the blocking session and whether it's a long-running transaction that needs to be addressed at the application level, not just killed reactively.
A service in GKE cannot connect to a dat: Work through layers systematically: confirm DNS resolves correctly from within a Pod (`nslookup`/`dig` from a debug Pod), confirm network routing/firewall rules allow the traffic (VPC firewall rules, and if crossing to a third-party endpoint, whether egress is allowed and if a Cloud NAT is configured for outbound internet access from private nodes), and confirm the application's own configuration (correct hostname/port, correct credentials) - testing connectivity directly with `curl`/`nc` from within a Pod isolates whether it's a network-layer or application-layer problem before going deeper into either.
What security controls would you add acr: CI/CD: mandatory SAST/dependency/secret scanning gates that block on findings. Containers: minimal base images, non-root users, image vulnerability scanning before deploy. Kubernetes: NetworkPolicies (default-deny), Pod Security Standards enforcement, RBAC least-privilege. Cloud IAM: scoped custom roles, Workload Identity instead of static keys, regular access reviews. Secrets: a dedicated secrets manager, never plaintext in code/config. Logging/audit: centralized, tamper-evident audit logs (Cloud Audit Logs, Kubernetes audit logs) retained long enough to support compliance and incident investigation - layering controls at every stage rather than relying on any single checkpoint.
Tell me about a time you automated a man: Structure as: the manual task and its cost (time spent, error rate, or toil it created), what you built to automate it, the measurable impact (time saved, incidents reduced, consistency improved), and how you shared it - documentation, a demo, or making it a reusable tool/template others could adopt rather than a one-off script only you know how to run - the sharing/knowledge-transfer part is often what distinguishes a genuinely impactful improvement from a personal productivity hack.
